text: GRC gets thrown around as a single buzzword so often that it's easy to forget it's actually shorthand for three genuinely different jobs. This lesson pulls them apart — governance, risk, and compliance — and then explains why a real program coordinates all three instead of running them as separate teams with separate spreadsheets.

Governance is about decision rights and accountability: who is authorized to accept a given risk, who owns a given control, who signs off before a new vendor touches customer data, and who's on the hook when something goes wrong. Risk management is the Chapter 3 practice — identifying, assessing, and treating risk. Compliance is different again: meeting obligations that come from outside the risk conversation entirely, like a regulation, a contract clause, or a board-approved policy. None of the three substitutes for either of the other two.

Here's the failure mode GRC exists to prevent. Three separate teams each maintain their own tracking sheet, each map the same handful of real controls to their own framework, and each ask the same control owner for the same evidence in a slightly different format. Nothing gets safer — it just gets more exhausting. A coordinated program instead treats governance, risk, and compliance as three views onto the same underlying controls and decisions, so one control gets assessed once and mapped to every framework it satisfies at the same time.

Most mature programs organize that accountability using the three lines of defense. The first line is operational management — the team that actually configures the control. The second line is the risk and compliance function, setting policy and independently challenging the first line's own assessment. The third line is internal audit, independent of both, verifying that the first two lines are actually doing what they claim.

Keep that structure in mind as you move into Lesson 2, because it's exactly what breaks down when an organization conflates its policy, standard, and procedure documents into one flat pile — which is where a lot of real GRC programs quietly start losing their accountability trail.
